sections.text: Your freelance hourly rate is the revenue you need in a year divided by the hours you can actually bill, and the second number is almost always smaller than people expect. In the example below, a freelancer who wants the equivalent of a $70,000 salary needs about $103,632 of revenue a year. Billing 24 hours a week for 46 weeks, that is $93.87 an hour, 2.79 times the $33.65 you get by dividing $70,000 by 2,080 working hours. The difference is unbilled time, business costs, benefits and self-employment tax. This guide shows the formula and which inputs move it.

items: Target income: the pre-income-tax salary you want, the same figure you would compare with a job offer.
Benefits you now buy yourself: health insurance and retirement contributions.
Business expenses: software, equipment, insurance, accounting, anything you must pay to work.

Self-employment tax: the IRS lists the rate as 15.3%, made up of 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare, and lets you deduct the employer-equivalent half when figuring income tax. The Self-Employment Tax Calculator on this site applies the rate to a reduced base of net earnings, so using 15.3% of full net profit here is a cautious simplification.
Billable hours: weeks worked x hours per week x the share of those hours you can invoice.

sections.text: Required revenue = business expenses + (target income + benefits) / (1 - 0.153). Hourly rate = required revenue / billable hours. Income tax is left out because your target is a pre-tax figure, like a salary.

items: Target income $70,000. Health insurance $6,000 a year and retirement contributions $5,000 a year are assumptions; use your own quotes.
Business expenses $8,000 a year, also an assumption.
46 working weeks (52 minus 6 weeks for vacation, holidays and sick time), 40 hours a week at work, 60% of those hours billable: 24 hours a week, 1,104 hours a year.
No state or local taxes, no unpaid invoices, and no income variation between months.

sections.text: Profit needed before self-employment tax: ($70,000 + $6,000 + $5,000) / 0.847 = $95,632, of which $14,632 is self-employment tax. Add $8,000 of expenses for required revenue of $103,632. Dividing by 1,104 hours gives $93.87 an hour. As a check, $93.87 x 1,104 = $103,632; subtracting expenses leaves $95,632; subtracting self-employment tax, health insurance and retirement leaves exactly $70,000.
Billable share is the biggest lever

Selling and administration, proposals, invoicing, learning and gaps between projects are real work, but not billable. A new freelancer who can bill half the week needs a rate about 20% higher than one who bills 60%. Track a month of actual hours before committing to a percentage.

rows: 5% of revenue lost to discounts or unpaid invoices

sections.text: Time off matters more than small expenses: going from 50 to 42 working weeks raises the rate by $16.45, while an extra $2,000 of expenses adds $1.81.
What a lower rate actually pays

headers: After self-employment tax, health and retirement

sections.text: The last column is before income tax. At $50 an hour, the same schedule leaves about $28,978 to live on, well under half the $70,000 target. To earn $103,632 at $60 an hour you would need 1,727 billable hours, 37.5 a week for 46 weeks, which leaves no time for finding work.

Use the hourly rate as your floor. A 20-hour project at $93.87 costs $1,877.40 if billed hourly. A fixed fee should be at least your estimated hours times your rate plus a buffer for revisions, because overruns come out of your pay. Charging more than the floor because the work is valuable to the client is reasonable, but you cannot know the value without asking, and a fee below the floor means you are subsidizing the project.

items: Dividing a salary by 2,080 hours and calling it a rate.
Assuming every working hour can be billed.
Forgetting that you now pay both halves of the Social Security and Medicare tax. Set aside money for quarterly estimated taxes; a tax professional can confirm the right amounts for you.
Ignoring benefits you used to get: paid leave, employer retirement contributions and insurance.
Never revisiting the rate. Re-run the numbers when expenses, hours or targets change.

sections.text: This model is for U.S.-style self-employment tax and a single rate. Other countries have different taxes, and clients, agencies and projects may set rates you cannot negotiate. Market rates also limit what you can charge. If your computed rate is far above what clients pay, the answer may be to lower costs, raise billable hours, or reconsider the target, not to ignore the math. The Salary to Hourly Calculator converts a salary into an hourly figure, the Self-Employment Tax Calculator estimates the tax, and a tax professional can confirm how rules apply to you.
